country.name: Greece
country.summary: Greece is an ancient wine country with a modern face. Its vines grow from the cool mountains of Macedonia to the volcanic ash of Santorini and the terraces of Samos, almost all of it on native grapes: Assyrtiko, Xinomavro, Agiorgitiko, Moschofilero, Malagousia, Roditis, Savatiano, Robola, Mavrodaphne, the Muscats and dozens more. The law is the European one, PDO and PGI, with Reserve and Grande Reserve as national ageing terms and Retsina as a traditional designation. The exam leans on four places: Santorini for Assyrtiko, Naoussa for Xinomavro, Nemea for Agiorgitiko and Mantinia for Moschofilero, with Samos and Patras for sweet wine, and asks the grape, the place and the style of each. Say the names with the stress on the right syllable and the table is yours.
country.overview:
Greece was growing and shipping wine when most of Europe was forest. The amphorae of Chios, Lesbos and Thasos went out across the ancient Mediterranean, and the pine resin that sealed them left the taste that survives as Retsina. The Byzantine and Venetian centuries kept the trade alive, the sweet Malvasia that passed through the port of Monemvasia carried its name across Europe, and the long Ottoman period let the vineyards sink to village wine. Phylloxera reached Greece late, in the 1890s in Macedonia, and Santorini's ash never saw it. The modern story begins with the national appellation law of 1969 and the first decrees of 1971, with Greece's entry into the European Community in 1981, and with a generation of estates from the 1980s that replaced bulk and resin with Naoussa, Nemea and Santorini on the world's lists.

The geography is mountains and sea. Macedonia in the north is cool and continental: Naoussa, Amyndeon and Goumenissa on and around Mount Vermio and Mount Paiko, Epanomi and the Slopes of Meliton towards the coast, Drama and Kavala to the east. Thessaly holds Rapsani under Olympus. Epirus has Zitsa's Debina in the mountains of the west. The Peloponnese holds Nemea's Agiorgitiko, Mantinia's Moschofilero on the Arcadian plateau and the sweet Muscat and Mavrodaphne of Patras. Attica around Athens is Savatiano and Retsina country. The Aegean gives Santorini's Assyrtiko on volcanic ash, Samos's Muscat on terraces, and Lemnos, Paros and Rhodes; the Ionian gives Kefalonia's Robola; and Crete, the largest island, keeps its own grapes, Vidiano, Vilana, Liatiko and Kotsifali, in Peza, Archanes, Dafnes and Sitia.

The law follows the European shape. The top tier is PDO, in Greek Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis, thirty three of them, which replaced the old OPAP seal for dry and the OPE seal for sweet appellation wines; below it PGI, Prostatevomeni Geografiki Endeixi, the former regional wines, by region, prefecture or district; then varietal wine and plain wine. Retsina and Verdea stand apart as traditional designations. Reserve and Grande Reserve are national ageing terms for PDO wines, with four years the agreed floor for a Grande Reserve red; Cava is the equivalent term for wine without an appellation. Ktima is estate.

The exam leans on the grapes and their homes. Assyrtiko and Santorini: kouloura baskets, own-rooted vines, salt and acid, Nykteri and Vinsanto. Xinomavro and Naoussa: acid black, the Nebbiolo decoy, with Amyndeon, Goumenissa and Rapsani as its cousins. Agiorgitiko and Nemea: St George's grape, soft and plummy, the Peloponnese. Moschofilero and Mantinia: pink-skinned, aromatic, high altitude. Samos for fortified Muscat, Patras for Mavrodaphne, Malagousia for the rescue story, Retsina for the footnote. Hold those and the rest of Greece is detail.
ladder: The protected designation of origin: thirty three appellations, each with a delimited zone, fixed grapes and rules, from Naoussa to Samos. It replaced the OPAP seal for dry wines and the OPE seal for sweet wines that the 1971 decrees created.

The protected geographical indication, the former Topikos Oinos or regional wine: by region (Peloponnese, Macedonia, Thessaly), by prefecture (Imathia, Florina, Corinth) or by district, with looser grape rules; where rosé, blends and international grapes go.
Wine without a geographical indication, which may still name a grape and a vintage; the former epitrapezios oinos, table wine.

Retsina, wine flavoured with Aleppo pine resin, chiefly Savatiano and Roditis from Attica and central Greece, and Verdea of Zakynthos, carry the term Onomasia kata Paradosi, appellation by tradition, rather than a PDO or PGI.

National ageing terms for PDO wines, Epilegmenos and Eidika Epilegmenos. As the standard references read the national rule: Reserve red two years with at least twelve months in oak and six in bottle, Reserve white one year with six in oak and three in bottle; Grande Reserve red four years with at least eighteen months in oak and eighteen in bottle, Grande Reserve white two years with twelve in oak and six in bottle. Older study guides carry an earlier arithmetic; four years for a Grande Reserve red is the number every version shares.
The ageing term for wine without a PDO: at least one year for a white and three for a red, part of it in oak; nothing to do with Spain's sparkling wine.
Ktima, estate, and words such as Monastiri, monastery, and Archontiko, mansion, may be used by a producer for wine from its own vineyards and winery under set conditions.
labels: dry, off dry, medium sweet, sweet

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.styles: The great white of Santorini and now of the mainland: searing acid, salt, lemon pith and stone, bone dry and ageworthy, and sun-dried into Vinsanto.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.styles: Acid black, the red of Macedonia: pale, tannic, high in acid, tomato, olive and dried rose, long-lived; alone at Naoussa and Amyndeon, blended at Goumenissa and Rapsani.

grapes.name: Agiorgitiko
grapes.styles: St George's grape, the most planted Greek red and Nemea's only grape: deep colour, plum and spice, soft tannin, from rosé to Grande Reserve and sweet wine.

grapes.name: Moschofilero
grapes.styles: Pink-skinned and aromatic, Mantinia's grape on the high Arcadian plateau: rose, citrus and spice, low alcohol, high acid, dry white and pale rosé.

grapes.name: Malagousia
grapes.styles: Rescued from near extinction from the 1970s, first in Chalkidiki and then at an estate at Epanomi near Thessaloniki: peach, jasmine and mint, moderate acid, the aromatic white of the mainland's estates.

grapes.name: Roditis
grapes.styles: Pink-skinned and widely planted, the workhorse white of the Peloponnese and Attica and a partner in Retsina; crisp and simple, better at altitude.

grapes.name: Savatiano
grapes.styles: The most planted Greek white, the grape of Attica and of Retsina, drought-resistant and low in acid, now also made as a serious old-vine dry white.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moschato Aspro, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains: the sweet wines of Samos, Patras, Rio Patras, Kefalonia and Rhodes, fortified or sun-dried, grapey and orange-scented; Lemnos's Muscat is the Alexandria kind.

grapes.name: Mavrodaphne
grapes.styles: The black laurel red of Patras and Kefalonia, made chiefly into fortified sweet wine aged for years in cask, and increasingly into dry red.

grapes.name: Robola
grapes.styles: Kefalonia's white on bare limestone: lemon, stone and high acid, dry; not the Ribolla Gialla of Friuli, whatever the name suggests.

grapes.name: Vidiano
grapes.styles: Crete's rising white: apricot, peach and herbs with good acidity, the island's answer to the mainland's aromatic whites.

grapes.name: Liatiko
grapes.styles: An ancient pale red of Crete, early-ripening, making soft dry reds and the island's traditional sweet wine from dried grapes.

grapes.name: Limnio
grapes.styles: One of the oldest named grapes, said to be the Lemnia of the ancient writers, from Lemnos and now Chalkidiki: medium-bodied, herbal and sage-scented red.

grapes.name: Athiri
grapes.styles: A soft, low-acid Aegean white, Assyrtiko's blending partner on Santorini and Rhodes.

grapes.name: Debina
grapes.styles: The white of Zitsa in Epirus, light, apple-scented and high in acid, made still and sparkling.

exam: The four grapes and their homes: Assyrtiko and Santorini, Xinomavro and Naoussa, Agiorgitiko and Nemea, Moschofilero and Mantinia.
Sweet Greece: Samos and Patras Muscat, Mavrodaphne of Patras, Vinsanto of Santorini; which is fortified and which sun-dried.
The law words: PDO and PGI in Greek, OPAP and OPE as history, Reserve and Grande Reserve, Cava, Retsina as a traditional designation, Ktima.
The Xinomavro family: Naoussa alone, Amyndeon alone with rosé and sparkling, Goumenissa with Negoska, Rapsani with Krassato and Stavroto.
The map: Macedonia in the north, Thessaly below it, Epirus in the west, the Peloponnese in the south, Attica around Athens, the Aegean and Ionian islands, Crete at the bottom.
Santorini's viticulture: kouloura baskets, own-rooted vines on ash, the meltemi, no phylloxera, Nykteri and Vinsanto.
Dates: the 1969 law, the 1971 first decrees, 1981 for the European Community; Retsina as the footnote and Malagousia's rescue as the modern story.
traps: Vinsanto, one word, is Santorini's sun-dried Assyrtiko; Vin Santo, two words, is Tuscany's; neither is fortified.
Samos Vin Doux and Mavrodaphne of Patras are fortified; Vinsanto and Samos Nectar are sun-dried and unfortified.
Robola is not Ribolla Gialla, Moschofilero is not a Muscat, and Malagousia is not a Muscat either, however aromatic.
Xinomavro is Macedonia's red and Agiorgitiko is the Peloponnese's; the exam swaps their homes and their descriptions.
Greece's Cava is an ageing term for wine without an appellation; it has nothing to do with Spanish sparkling wine.
Retsina is a traditional designation, not a PDO or a PGI, and the resin goes into the fermenting must; it does not come from resinated barrels.
Macedonia in Greek wine means the northern Greek region; the neighbouring country is North Macedonia.
Older study guides carry older Reserve arithmetic; four years for a Grande Reserve red is the number every version agrees on.

cards.f: Greece's four exam grapes and their homes
cards.b: Assyrtiko: Santorini. Xinomavro: Naoussa. Agiorgitiko: Nemea. Moschofilero: Mantinia.

cards.f: Greek PDO in Greek, and what it replaced
cards.b: Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis, POP; thirty three of them. It replaced OPAP, the dry appellation seal, and OPE, the sweet one, from the 1971 decrees.

cards.f: Grande Reserve red: the number every source agrees on
cards.b: Four years before release, split between oak and bottle. Reserve is shorter; whites need less than reds. Epilegmenos is Reserve, Eidika Epilegmenos is Grande Reserve.

cards.f: Fortified or sun-dried? Greece's sweet wines
cards.b: Fortified: Samos Vin Doux, Mavrodaphne of Patras, and Muscat of Patras as a rule. Sun-dried, unfortified: Santorini Vinsanto, Samos Nectar.

cards.f: Retsina: grape, resin, status
cards.b: Savatiano mostly, with Roditis; Aleppo pine resin added during fermentation; a traditional designation, Onomasia kata Paradosi, not a PDO; Attica is its home.

cards.f: Greece's Xinomavro appellations
cards.b: Naoussa: alone, red. Amyndeon: alone, red, rosé, sparkling. Goumenissa: with Negoska, 20% minimum. Rapsani: with Krassato and Stavroto, equal parts.

cards.f: Three Greek dates
cards.b: 1969: the national appellation law. 1971: the first appellation decrees, Naoussa, Nemea and Rapsani among them. 1981: Greece joins the European Community.

cards.f: False friends of Greek wine
cards.b: Vinsanto is not Vin Santo. Robola is not Ribolla Gialla. Moschofilero and Malagousia are not Muscats. Greek Cava is an ageing term, not sparkling wine.

cards.f: The Malagousia story
cards.b: A nearly extinct aromatic white, rescued from the 1970s by a winemaker in Chalkidiki and planted at his estate at Epanomi near Thessaloniki; now a national white of peach, jasmine and mint. The standard rescue-story answer.

questions.q: Which grape is the most planted red variety in Greece?
questions.exp: Agiorgitiko, Nemea's grape, is Greece's most planted red. Xinomavro leads Macedonia, Mavrodaphne is the fortified grape of Patras, and Liatiko is Cretan.

questions.q: Which resin is added to Retsina during fermentation?
questions.exp: Retsina takes Aleppo pine resin added to the fermenting must, mostly on Savatiano from Attica. Mastic, the resin of Chios, goes into a liqueur, and cypress and juniper flavour no Greek wine.

questions.q: Which grape makes the aromatic white wines of Mantinia?
questions.exp: Mantinia on the Arcadian plateau is Moschofilero, a pink-skinned aromatic grape pressed to a pale, rose-scented dry white; it is not a Muscat.

questions.q: What is the minimum total ageing for a Greek PDO red wine labelled Grande Reserve?
questions.exp: A Grande Reserve red needs four years before release, part in oak and part in bottle; this is the one number the old and the current readings of the rule share.

questions.q: Which island is famous for its fortified sweet Muscat?
questions.exp: Samos makes Vin Doux and Grand Cru from Muscat Blanc on terraces up Mount Ampelos. Santorini's sweet wine is sun-dried Vinsanto, Crete's is Liatiko, and Paros makes Monemvasia white and Mandilaria red.

questions.q: Which grape makes the dry white wines of Santorini?
questions.exp: Santorini is Assyrtiko, the great majority of the blend with Athiri and Aidani permitted, grown own-rooted in kouloura baskets on volcanic ash.

questions.q: Which Greek sweet wine is made from sun-dried Assyrtiko?
questions.exp: Vinsanto, one word, is Santorini's sweet wine from sun-dried Assyrtiko with Aidani, unfortified and aged for years in cask; Tuscany's Vin Santo is two words and unrelated. Samos Nectar is sun-dried Muscat, and the two Patras wines are fortified.

questions.q: In which year did Greece's first wine appellation decrees come into force?
questions.exp: The national appellation law of 1969 produced the first decrees in 1971, Naoussa, Nemea and Rapsani among them; 1981 is the year Greece joined the European Community.

regions.name: Naoussa
regions.summary: Naoussa is the reference appellation for Xinomavro and the red the exam treats as Greece's answer to Nebbiolo. It lies in Imathia in Central Macedonia, on the eastern and south-eastern foothills of Mount Vermio west of Thessaloniki, and has carried its own appellation since the first Greek decrees of 1971. The wine is dry red from Xinomavro alone: pale in colour, high in acid, firmly tannic, smelling of sun-dried tomato, olive, dried rose and spice, and built to age for decades. A continental climate softened by the mountain, soils that shift from clay and limestone to sand and schist, and a split between the traditional long-aged houses and a gentler young school give a server plenty to say.

terroir.climate: Continental with a Mediterranean cast: cold winters that can bring snow, warm summers and a long, dry ripening season running into October. Mount Vermio to the west takes the worst of the weather, the slopes face east and south-east into the morning sun, and the Thermaic Gulf, some way east, blunts the extremes. Rainfall is higher than on the islands and spring can be wet, so downy mildew is the standing threat and hail the occasional one. Xinomavro ripens late and needs every week of that autumn.
terroir.soils: A patchwork rather than one soil. The old core is calcareous clay-loam over limestone bedrock, which gives the firmest and longest-lived wines; the lower, eastern ground around Trilofos is sandier and lighter and gives softer Xinomavro that drinks sooner; and bands of schist and gravel show on the higher and western ground. Drainage is good almost everywhere, which matters for a rot-prone grape in a district with real rain.
terroir.topography: The vineyards lie on the eastern and south-eastern foothills of Mount Vermio in a belt roughly between 150 and 350 metres above sea level, with a few sites higher, around the town of Naoussa and a ring of villages. Altitude and aspect change the wine: the higher, cooler sites to the north and west ripen later and keep more acid and perfume, while the lower, warmer ground to the east and south gives fuller fruit and rounder tannin.
terroir.water: The Arapitsa, a mountain stream that drops through the town of Naoussa, once drove its textile mills and still marks the heart of the district; otherwise the vines live on Vermio's rain and snowmelt. The Aliakmonas, the longest river wholly in Greece, passes well to the south on its way to the Thermaic Gulf, and the gulf's breath is a distant moderating influence rather than a daily one.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.styles: The only grape the appellation allows: pale, high in acid, thick with tannin, and the source of the tomato leaf, olive, dried rose and spice that mark Naoussa; it fades to brick early and keeps for decades.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Grown beside Xinomavro for PGI Imathia and PGI Macedonia blends that soften the native grape's colour and tannin; never part of a wine labelled Naoussa.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: A second partner for Xinomavro in regional blends and a varietal under the PGI, warmer and darker than anything the appellation itself permits.

wines.note: Pale garnet turning to brick within a few years, with sour cherry, sun-dried tomato, black olive, dried rose and sweet spice, searing acidity and a firm grip. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees, decant a young bottle, and pour it with roast lamb, game birds, mushrooms or a tomato-rich braise.

Longer in cask and bottle before release: the tannin starts to soften and leather, tobacco and dried fig join the tomato and olive. The classic style of the old houses, and a wine for slow-cooked meat and aged cheese.

Four years' ageing at least, divided between cask and bottle, released tawny-edged with dried flowers, tar, dried tomato and a long savoury finish; the Greek bottle most often set beside an old Barolo at a blind tasting.

The modern school's wine: a short maceration, some whole bunches and little or no new oak give bright red cherry, tomato skin and rose over a lighter frame. Serve a touch cooler, around 15 degrees, with charcuterie, grilled vegetables or a lamb burger.

Rosé and sparkling Xinomavro and the Xinomavro blends with Merlot or Syrah leave the appellation and go out as PGI Imathia or PGI Macedonia; the rosé is pale, strawberry-scented and sharp, and a good aperitif.

made.viticulture: Xinomavro is a late ripener with big bunches, thin skins and a taste for vigour, so the whole year is about restraint and patience. Older plots stand as bush vines; most of the district is now on wires in cordon or Guyot, with the rows run across the slope and the canopy opened to the morning sun so the bunches dry after rain. Growers thin the crop in summer, because an overloaded Xinomavro vine will not ripen its tannin, and pick late, from the end of September through October, chasing phenolic ripeness while the acid is still high. The hazards are spring frost on the low ground, mildew and rot in a wet year, hail, and uneven ripening within a bunch. Site is the great choice: the higher, cooler villages to the west and north keep acid and perfume, the sandier eastern ground gives softer, earlier fruit, and old vines on the limestone core are prized above all.
made.winemaking: The grape sets the method. Xinomavro carries little colour pigment and a great deal of tannin, so extraction is the winemaker's main decision. The traditional school ferments in open vats, macerates for three or four weeks, and matures the wine in large old oak casks for a year or more, releasing it years later as Reserve or Grande Reserve when the colour has gone to brick and the tomato, olive and leather have come forward. The modern school, which took hold in the 2000s, picks a little earlier, uses whole bunches and gentler pump-overs, keeps maceration short, and ages in older or larger French oak so the red fruit and rose stay in front of the tannin. Both schools avoid chasing a deep colour that heavy extraction cannot give this grape anyway. Outside the appellation, blends with Merlot or Syrah, rosé by direct pressing and sparkling rosé take the surplus. The Reserve and Grande Reserve ageing terms are the national ones, not rules of the appellation itself.

law.classification: Naoussa is a protected designation of origin under European Union law, carried in Greek as Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis, and one of the appellations set up by the first Greek decrees of 1971 under the national appellation law of 1969. It covers dry red wine only, from Xinomavro alone, grown within a delimited zone of villages on the Vermio foothills in Imathia. There is no official ranking of vineyards or villages: a village or vineyard name on a label is the producer's choice, not a cru. The two ageing terms a bottle may carry, Reserve and Grande Reserve, are the national rules for PDO reds, with four years the floor for Grande Reserve. Everything else the district makes, Xinomavro rosé, sparkling Xinomavro, blends with international grapes and all white wine, is sold under the regional PGI Imathia or PGI Macedonia.

Dry red from 100% Xinomavro grown within the delimited villages on the eastern slopes of Vermio; no rosé, white or sparkling wine may carry the name.

The national Reserve term for a PDO red, Epilegmenos: an extended ageing in oak and bottle before release, shorter than Grande Reserve.
Naoussa Grande Reserve
The national Grande Reserve term for a PDO red, Eidika Epilegmenos: at least four years' ageing before release, divided between oak and bottle.
PGI Imathia and PGI Macedonia
The regional wines of the same slopes: Xinomavro blended with Merlot or Syrah, rosé and sparkling Xinomavro, and the whites; none may say Naoussa.

places.name: Mount Vermio
places.note: The mountain whose eastern and south-eastern foothills hold the whole appellation, shielding the vines from the west and giving them the morning sun; the villages of the zone ring its lower slopes between roughly 150 and 350 metres. Amyndeon lies on its other face.

places.name: Naoussa
places.note: The market town at the centre of the district, with the Arapitsa stream falling through it and the old family cellars in its streets; the house founded here in 1879 by Ioannis Boutaris carried the wine's name across Greece.

places.name: Paliokalias
places.note: A named old vineyard close to the town whose name appears on a single-site bottling from one of the town's oldest wine families: old vines, perfume and grip.

places.name: Yianakohori
places.note: A village on the high western ground, around 300 metres, on stony clay over limestone: the home of the Ramnista vineyard and of the most structured, longest-lived modern Naoussa, and the base of the Boutari family's second house.

places.name: Ramnista
places.note: The vineyard at Yianakohori whose name is the flagship Naoussa of its estate: tight, tannic, tomato leaf and dried rose, a wine that wants a decade.

places.name: Trilofos
places.note: A village on the lower, eastern side of the zone on sandier soils, which give a softer, earlier-drinking Xinomavro; the base of the house that made young-vine Naoussa a style of its own.

places.name: Fytia
places.note: Among the higher villages of the appellation, on the mountain's slopes above the town: later harvests, higher acid and a more floral, lifted Xinomavro.

places.name: Stenimachos
places.note: The village just below the town where the house founded in the town in 1879 built its modern winery; the lower, warmer ground of the zone and the source of much classic Grande Reserve.

places.name: Gastra
places.note: A small terraced site above the town where a one-family estate makes a single old-vine Naoussa of unusual purity, a name an Advanced candidate meets in a producer question rather than on a map.

producers.name: Boutari
producers.why: Founded at Naoussa in 1879 by Ioannis Boutaris, the house that made the appellation's name, and whose Grande Reserve is the classic old-school Naoussa on any list.

producers.name: Kir-Yianni
producers.why: Founded in 1997 at Yianakohori by a member of the Boutari family; Ramnista is the modern reference for structured Naoussa, and the house also farms Amyndeon, so one name holds the contrast between the two.

producers.name: Thymiopoulos Vineyards
producers.why: The Trilofos estate whose whole-bunch, low-extraction Young Vines Xinomavro showed that Naoussa could be drunk early, and whose Earth and Sky is the top old-vine bottling.

producers.name: Dalamara
producers.why: One of the oldest family cellars in Naoussa town, with a single-site Paliokalias that shows the perfumed, old-vine side of the district.

producers.name: Karydas
producers.why: A tiny estate at Gastra above the town making one pure Naoussa from old vines; the example of a one-wine grower in an Advanced producer question.

producers.name: Vaeni Naoussa
producers.why: The growers' cooperative of the district, founded in 1983, whose Naoussa and Grande Reserve are the honest, widely seen baseline of the appellation.

producers.name: Diamantakos
producers.why: A small family estate whose Naoussa and whose varietal Preknadi white show a precise, modern hand on both the appellation and the district's rarities.

producers.name: Foundi
producers.why: A family estate making traditional, cask-aged Naoussa and a Xinomavro rosé under the regional PGI, a good study of the two labels side by side.

producers.name: Chrisohoou
producers.why: A Naoussa family house whose traditional, long-aged Xinomavro keeps the old style alive beside its newer bottlings.

exam: The grape rule: Xinomavro alone, dry red only, and the meaning of the name, acid black.
The place: Imathia, Central Macedonia, the eastern foothills of Mount Vermio, west of Thessaloniki; not the Peloponnese.
The blind-tasting profile: pale garnet to brick, high acid, high tannin, sun-dried tomato, olive, dried rose, spice, and the Nebbiolo decoy.
The ageing terms: Reserve and Grande Reserve are national, four years at least for Grande Reserve red.
The year 1971, the first Greek appellation decrees, and the 1969 law behind them.
The two schools: traditional long maceration and old cask against the whole-bunch, early-drinking modern style, and the producers that stand for each.
Service: 16 to 18 degrees, a decant for a young wine, lamb, game, mushrooms and tomato-based dishes.
traps: Naoussa is red only: a Xinomavro rosé or sparkling wine from the same slopes is PGI Imathia or Macedonia, and Amyndeon is the appellation that allows them.
Pale colour is the grape, not a fault or a sign of a thin wine; Xinomavro's brick rim arrives early and says nothing about age or extraction.
Xinomavro is compared with Nebbiolo for structure and aroma, but Naoussa sits lower and warmer than Barolo and its tomato and olive note is its own; the comparison is not a claim of relation.
Rapsani uses Xinomavro too but blends it with Krassato and Stavroto; Goumenissa blends it with Negoska; only Naoussa and Amyndeon use it alone.
Macedonia here is the Greek region around Thessaloniki, not the neighbouring country to the north.
The Boutari firm and Kir-Yianni share a family origin but are separate companies with separate wines.
Reserve and Grande Reserve are national ageing terms, not Naoussa's own classification; the appellation ranks no vineyard.

cards.b: Acid black. Pale garnet to brick, high acid, high tannin, sun-dried tomato, olive, dried rose, spice; the Nebbiolo decoy.

cards.f: Naoussa Grande Reserve: the ageing floor
cards.b: Four years at least before release, divided between oak and bottle, under the national rule for PDO reds; Reserve is the shorter term. Both are national words, not Naoussa's own.

cards.f: Naoussa's appellation date and the law behind it
cards.b: 1971, among the first Greek appellation decrees, under the national appellation law of 1969; a PDO today.

cards.f: The four Xinomavro appellations and how each uses the grape
cards.b: Naoussa: alone, red. Amyndeon: alone, red, rosé and sparkling. Goumenissa: with at least 20% Negoska. Rapsani, in Thessaly, blends it with Krassato and Stavroto.

cards.f: Naoussa's two schools of winemaking
cards.b: Traditional: long maceration, years in old cask, Reserve and Grande Reserve. Modern: whole bunch, short maceration, older oak, drunk young with red fruit in front.

cards.f: Serving Naoussa: temperature, decant, dishes
cards.b: 16 to 18 degrees, decant a young bottle; roast lamb, game birds, mushrooms, tomato braises, aged cheese. Young-vine style a touch cooler.

questions.q: Which grape variety is permitted in a wine labelled Naoussa?
questions.exp: Naoussa is Xinomavro alone. Agiorgitiko is Nemea's grape in the Peloponnese, Negoska is the blending partner at Goumenissa, and Limnio is an ancient red of Lemnos and the Macedonian coast.

questions.q: On the foothills of which mountain do the vineyards of Naoussa lie?
questions.exp: Naoussa sits on the eastern slopes of Mount Vermio in Imathia. Olympus is Rapsani's mountain, Paiko stands above Goumenissa, and Kyllini rises west of Nemea.

questions.q: With which Italian grape is Xinomavro most often paired as a blind-tasting decoy?
questions.exp: Xinomavro and Nebbiolo share pale colour, high acid, high tannin, dried rose and tar, and a long life. Sangiovese is brighter and less tannic, Aglianico darker, and Nerello Mascalese is Etna's decoy for Pinot Noir.

questions.q: In which region of Greece does the Naoussa appellation lie?
questions.exp: Naoussa lies in Macedonia, the northern Greek region around Thessaloniki, not the country over the border; its regional unit is Imathia. Amyndeon in Florina and Goumenissa in Kilkis are the other Macedonian Xinomavro districts, and Nemea is in the Peloponnese.

questions.q: Which house, founded at Naoussa in 1879, made the appellation's name across Greece?
questions.exp: Boutari was founded at Naoussa in 1879 and made the appellation's name; Kir-Yianni, founded in 1997 at Yianakohori by a member of the same family, is a separate house. Tsantali is the Macedonian firm that revived Rapsani, and Gaia Wines works Nemea and Santorini.

questions.q: What does the grape name Xinomavro mean in English?
questions.exp: Xino is sour or acid and mavro is black: the name describes the grape's high acidity and dark skin, though the wine it makes is pale.

questions.q: Which style of wine may carry the Naoussa appellation?
questions.exp: Naoussa is a dry red appellation only. Rosé and sparkling Xinomavro are permitted at Amyndeon, and sweet red is a Nemea tradition, not a Naoussa one.

questions.q: Which pair of aromas is the classic signature of a mature Naoussa?
questions.exp: Mature Xinomavro smells of sun-dried tomato, black olive, dried rose and spice. Gooseberry and grass say Sauvignon Blanc, blackcurrant and cedar say Cabernet, and lychee says Gewürztraminer.

regions.name: Amyndeon
regions.summary: Amyndeon, also written Amynteo and Amyntaio, is the coldest appellation in Greece and among the highest: a plateau at roughly 570 to 750 metres in Florina, Western Macedonia, ringed by mountains and set between four lakes. Its grape is Xinomavro alone, as at Naoussa, but here the appellation covers dry red, still rosé and sparkling rosé, so Amyndeon is the name a sommelier reaches for when Greek rosé or sparkling rosé comes up. Sandy soils let old vines stand on their own roots, winters bring snow and spring frost, and the red is paler, higher-toned and earlier-drinking than Naoussa's. The appellation dates from 1972, a year after its neighbour over the mountain.

terroir.climate: The coldest wine climate in Greece. The plateau's winters fall well below freezing with snow, spring frost is a real danger, summers are warm but short, and the nights are cool enough to make the diurnal swing the district's great asset for acidity and aroma. Harvest runs into October, among the latest in the country. The four lakes store summer heat and give it back on cold nights, and northerly winds keep the air moving. Rain is moderate and comes mainly outside the growing season.
terroir.soils: Sand over limestone, mixed with the deposits of the old lake basin: light, poor, quick-draining soil that phylloxera cannot tunnel, which is why old own-rooted Xinomavro survives here and why Kali Riza, good root, is a vineyard name. Clay appears in patches near the lakes and gives a little more flesh; the sand gives perfume and a lighter frame.
terroir.topography: A high basin on the edge of Western Macedonia, with Mount Vermio closing the south-east and Mount Vitsi the west, and the vineyards spread on gentle slopes and lake terraces between about 570 and 750 metres. There is little dramatic relief; altitude, exposure to the lakes and the cold-air drainage of a site decide the frost risk and the ripening.
terroir.water: Four lakes: Vegoritida, the largest and deepest, with Petron beside it, and the smaller Zazari and Cheimaditida to the west. They moderate the plateau's extremes, soften frost on the shoreline sites and add humidity to the cool nights; the village of Xino Nero, sour water, takes its name from a naturally sparkling spring.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.styles: The single permitted grape, grown on sand and often own-rooted: lighter in body and colour than at Naoussa, with raspberry, strawberry, tomato leaf and rose, and acidity that makes it a natural rosé and sparkling base.

grapes.name: Roditis
grapes.styles: A pink-skinned white grown on the plateau for regional whites and blends under PGI Florina, crisp and lemony at this altitude.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The international white that took to the cool plateau, grown for PGI Florina and blended with Roditis by one leading house.

grapes.name: Malagousia
grapes.styles: The revived aromatic Greek white, planted by the plateau's estates for peach and jasmine scented PGI whites with the altitude's acidity.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: An international red of the plateau's estates, sold under PGI Florina in varietal and blended wines outside the appellation.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: A cool-climate newcomer that some estates planted on the plateau's sand with real success, outside the appellation.

wines.note: Pale ruby, lighter and brighter than Naoussa: raspberry, strawberry, tomato leaf, rose and a stony edge, with high acid and a tannin that is firm but not fierce. Serve at 15 to 16 degrees with grilled lamb, charcuterie or a tomato and feta dish.

The classic dry Greek rosé: Xinomavro pressed or briefly macerated to a pale pink, strawberry, pomegranate and herbs, with sharp acidity. Serve cold as an aperitif or with grilled fish, octopus and meze.

Xinomavro's acidity and pale colour make it a natural base: tank-method sparkling rosé is the volume style, dry or semi-dry, and a few houses make traditional-method brut, with wild strawberry, rose and a dry, savoury finish. A sparkling to open a Greek dinner.

Old-vine, own-rooted Xinomavro aged in oak under the national Reserve term: more depth and dried-flower complexity on the same high-toned frame, and the plateau's best argument for Xinomavro's age-worthiness in a cool site.
The regional wines of the plateau: Sauvignon Blanc, Malagousia, Roditis and Chardonnay whites, and Syrah, Merlot and Pinot Noir reds, from the estates that use the appellation only for Xinomavro.

made.viticulture: The plateau sets the choices. Old plots are bush vines on sand, many on their own roots because phylloxera cannot move through such soil, and some of those vines are very old; newer vineyards go on wires with vertical shoot positioning so the canopy can be opened to the sun in a cool year. Frost is the first enemy: growers favour slopes with air drainage and sites near the lakes, and a late spring frost can take much of a crop. Ripening is the second: Xinomavro ripens late, and on the plateau the harvest runs into October, among the latest in Greece, so a cool year may not bring the tannin fully ripe. That is the logic of the rosé and the sparkling wine: fruit that would make a hard red makes a fine rosé or a bright sparkling base. Yields are kept modest, the crop is thinned, and picking is by hand in the cold mornings of autumn.
made.winemaking: Three wines from one grape. The rosé is made by direct pressing or a few hours of skin contact, fermented cool in steel and bottled young for its strawberry and acid. The sparkling wine is mostly made by the tank method for freshness, with a few houses working the traditional method on Xinomavro, bottle-fermented and aged on lees for a drier, more savoury wine; some press the grape white for a blanc de noirs. The red is handled more gently than at Naoussa: shorter macerations, cooler fermentation, older or larger oak, and an eye on keeping the aroma and the pale colour the sand gives rather than forcing extraction. Reserve wines from old own-rooted vines go longer in French oak under the national terms. Outside the appellation the estates work the international grapes conventionally in steel and barrique for the regional PGI.

law.classification: Amyndeon is a protected designation of origin set up in 1972, a year after Naoussa, in the Florina regional unit of Western Macedonia. The grape is Xinomavro alone. Unlike Naoussa, the appellation covers more than one style: dry red, dry still rosé, and sparkling rosé, dry or semi-dry, which makes it the Greek appellation to name for rosé and the only one whose Xinomavro may be sparkling. Reserve and Grande Reserve are the national ageing terms. The international varieties and the whites the same estates grow are sold under the regional PGI Florina or PGI Macedonia, and a Xinomavro that fails to ripen for the appellation may take the same route.

Dry red from 100% Xinomavro grown on the plateau; lighter and higher-toned than Naoussa and the comparison the exam likes.
Amyndeon PDO rosé
Dry still rosé from Xinomavro: the Greek PDO rosé a sommelier should be able to name.
Amyndeon PDO sparkling rosé
Sparkling rosé from Xinomavro, dry or semi-dry, by tank or traditional method: the only Greek appellation sparkling wine from this grape.
Reserve and Grande Reserve
The national ageing terms for PDO wine, Epilegmenos and Eidika Epilegmenos; four years at least for a Grande Reserve red.
PGI Florina
The regional wine of the prefecture: the plateau's Sauvignon Blanc, Malagousia, Syrah, Merlot and Pinot Noir, and any Xinomavro sold outside the appellation.

places.name: The Amyndeon plateau
places.note: The whole appellation: a high basin at 570 to 750 metres in Florina, ringed by Vermio and Vitsi, with the vineyards on sandy slopes and lake terraces around the town and the four lakes.

places.name: Amyndeon
places.note: The town at the centre of the plateau and the seat of the growers' cooperative, whose rosé and sparkling rosé were for decades the only Amyndeon most of Greece saw.

places.name: Agios Panteleimon
places.note: A village on the southern shore of Lake Vegoritida around 620 metres, on sand and lake terraces: the base of the estate that put single-vineyard, old-vine Amyndeon Xinomavro on the world's lists.

places.name: Xino Nero
places.note: Sour water: a village named for its naturally sparkling spring, a short way from the town, with old own-rooted vines on sand and a long cooperative history.

places.name: Lake Vegoritida
places.note: The largest of the four lakes, deep and cold, lying along the eastern side of the basin below Mount Vermio; its shoreline sites feel the water's moderation most.

places.name: Petres and Lake Petron
places.note: The village and the smaller lake beside Vegoritida, in the heart of the basin, with vineyards on the sandy rises between the two lakes.

places.name: Mount Vermio
places.note: The same mountain that holds Naoussa on its eastern face; Amyndeon lies on its north-western side, a few hundred metres higher and several degrees colder, which is the whole story of the two appellations.

producers.name: Alpha Estate
producers.why: Founded in 1997 at Agios Panteleimon, the estate whose single-block, old-vine Xinomavro and plateau-grown international varieties made Amyndeon a name on fine wine lists.

producers.name: Kir-Yianni
producers.why: The Naoussa house that also farms the plateau: Kali Riza from own-rooted vines on sand and Akakies, the sparkling rosé, make the Naoussa and Amyndeon contrast concrete under one name.

producers.name: Karanika
producers.why: A small estate devoted to traditional-method sparkling wine from Xinomavro on the plateau, the reference for serious bottle-fermented Greek sparkling from this grape.

producers.name: The Amyndeon Wine Cooperative
producers.why: The growers' cooperative in the town, for decades the whole appellation's output, and still the source of the straightforward rosé, sparkling rosé and red that define the category at a tavern price.

exam: The one-grape, three-style rule: Xinomavro alone for dry red, still rosé and sparkling rosé.
The geography that explains the style: Florina, Western Macedonia, 570 to 750 metres, four lakes, Greece's coldest appellation and among its highest, harvest in October.
Sand, own-rooted vines and why phylloxera cannot cross them.
Amyndeon against Naoussa: the same grape on the two faces of Vermio, paler, fresher and earlier here, firmer and longer-lived there.
The appellation year, 1972, and the producers that stand for the plateau.
Service: red at 15 to 16 degrees, rosé cold, sparkling rosé as the aperitif of a Greek dinner.
traps: Amyndeon, Amynteo and Amyntaio are one place; do not treat the spellings as different appellations.
Naoussa is red only; Amyndeon is the Xinomavro appellation that allows rosé and sparkling, and the one to name for Greek PDO rosé.
Own-rooted does not mean old by itself; the sand keeps phylloxera out, and many plateau vines are young plantings on their own roots.
The four lakes moderate the climate but the plateau is still the coldest in Greece; it is altitude, not latitude, that makes it so.
Kali Riza is a vineyard and wine name, good root, not a grape and not a village.
Florina is the regional unit; Amyndeon is the town, the plateau and the appellation; Western Macedonia is the administrative region.

cards.f: Amyndeon: the grape and the three styles the appellation allows
cards.b: Xinomavro alone. Dry red, dry still rosé, and sparkling rosé, dry or semi-dry. It is the Greek appellation to name for rosé and for sparkling Xinomavro.

cards.f: Amyndeon: where, how high, how cold
cards.b: Florina, Western Macedonia, a plateau at about 570 to 750 metres between four lakes: the coldest appellation in Greece and among the highest, harvest into October.

cards.f: Why are many Amyndeon vines own-rooted?
cards.b: Sandy soils over limestone and old lake deposits; phylloxera cannot move through sand, so Xinomavro survives ungrafted, and Kali Riza, good root, names a vineyard of such vines.

cards.f: Name the four lakes of Amyndeon
cards.b: Vegoritida, the largest; Petron beside it; Zazari and Cheimaditida to the west. They moderate frost and heat on the plateau.

cards.f: Amyndeon against Naoussa in the glass
cards.b: Same grape, two faces of Vermio. Amyndeon: paler, raspberry and rose, lighter tannin, earlier drinking. Naoussa: firmer, tomato and olive, longer-lived.

cards.f: Amyndeon: appellation year and the house that made its name abroad
cards.b: 1972, a year after Naoussa. Alpha Estate, founded in 1997 at Agios Panteleimon on Lake Vegoritida, built the plateau's reputation abroad on old-vine, single-block Xinomavro.

cards.f: Serving Amyndeon rosé and sparkling rosé
cards.b: Rosé cold, 8 to 10 degrees, with meze, grilled fish and octopus. Sparkling rosé as the aperitif of a Greek dinner: strawberry, rose, dry savoury finish.

questions.q: Which Greek appellation permits Xinomavro to be made as a sparkling rosé?
questions.exp: Amyndeon covers red, still rosé and sparkling rosé from Xinomavro. Naoussa and Goumenissa are dry red only, and Rapsani is a dry red blend of three grapes.

questions.q: In which regional unit of Greece does the Amyndeon appellation lie?
questions.exp: Amyndeon is in Florina in Western Macedonia. Imathia holds Naoussa, Kilkis holds Goumenissa and Larissa holds Rapsani in Thessaly.

questions.q: Which grape variety is permitted in the wines of Amyndeon?
questions.exp: Amyndeon, like Naoussa, is Xinomavro alone; the difference is that Amyndeon may make rosé and sparkling wine as well as red from it.

questions.q: Why do old vines on the Amyndeon plateau often grow on their own roots?
opts: The soils are sandy and phylloxera cannot spread through sand
The altitude is too high for the louse to survive the winter
The vines are a resistant hybrid of Xinomavro
Grafting is forbidden by the appellation's rules
questions.exp: Phylloxera cannot tunnel through loose sand, so Amyndeon's sandy soils, like Santorini's ash, keep ungrafted Xinomavro alive. Altitude, hybrids and the appellation rules have nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Roughly how high do the vineyards of Amyndeon lie?
questions.exp: The Amyndeon plateau sits at about 570 to 750 metres, among the highest appellation vineyards in Greece and the reason for its late harvest and bright acidity.

questions.q: How does a red Amyndeon usually compare with a Naoussa in the glass?
questions.exp: Amyndeon sits on the colder, higher north-western face of Vermio on sand, so its Xinomavro is paler, higher-toned and readier than Naoussa's firmer, longer-lived wine. No Xinomavro appellation is sweet or fortified, and the plateau uses oak more gently than Naoussa's old school, not more.

questions.q: In which year was the Amyndeon appellation established?
questions.exp: Amyndeon followed Naoussa by a year: Naoussa, Nemea and Rapsani were among the first decrees of 1971, Amyndeon came in 1972 and Goumenissa in 1979.

regions.name: Goumenissa
regions.summary: Goumenissa is the third Xinomavro appellation of Greek Macedonia and the one that blends. It lies in the Kilkis regional unit north-west of Thessaloniki, on the south-eastern foothills of Mount Paiko above the plain of the Axios river, and has been an appellation since 1979. The rule is Xinomavro with at least 20% Negoska, a local grape that brings colour, flesh and alcohol to Xinomavro's acid and tannin, so the wine is rounder and readier than Naoussa and darker in the glass. Lower, warmer and smaller than its two cousins, it is a district of a few family estates and one large house, and the blending rule is the fact a Certified candidate must hold.

terroir.climate: Continental in its winters and Mediterranean in its summers, warmer than Naoussa and much warmer than Amyndeon, with the Axios plain opening to the south-east and the Thermaic Gulf beyond it. The Vardaris, the cold north wind that funnels down the Axios valley, dries the vineyards after rain and keeps rot in check but can chill a spring. Rain is moderate and summers are dry, so Negoska ripens fully and Xinomavro loses some of its hardest edges.
terroir.soils: Clay and sandy loam over limestone on the foothills, with stonier, better-drained ground higher up Paiko and heavier clay towards the plain; a soil that gives Negoska its flesh and lets Xinomavro ripen a little more generously than on Naoussa's limestone core.
terroir.topography: The south-eastern slopes of Mount Paiko, a broad wooded massif north-west of Thessaloniki, falling to the Axios plain; the vineyards lie around the town of Goumenissa and the villages above it at a modest altitude, lower than Naoussa and far lower than Amyndeon, on gentle slopes and terraces facing the morning sun.
terroir.water: The Axios, the Vardar of the north, crosses the plain to the east on its way to the Thermaic Gulf and gives the valley its wind; streams off Paiko water the town, which grew on its mills and its brass bands rather than on the vine alone.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.styles: The senior partner, up to 80% of the blend: acid, tannin, tomato leaf and dried rose, a little riper here than at Naoussa on warmer, lower ground.

grapes.name: Negoska
grapes.styles: Named for Negush, the old Slavic name of Naoussa, and grown almost nowhere else: deep colour, lower acid, higher alcohol and soft tannin, which is exactly what Xinomavro lacks. At least 20% of a Goumenissa.

grapes.name: Roditis
grapes.styles: The pink-skinned white of the district's regional wines, crisp and simple under PGI Macedonia.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.styles: Planted by estates for regional whites, where its acidity suits the warm foothills; never part of the appellation.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: An international red grown for PGI Macedonia blends and varietals alongside the native pair.

wines.note: Medium ruby, deeper than Naoussa, with sour cherry, plum, tomato leaf, dried herbs and sweet spice, fresh acid and a rounder, riper tannin. Serve at 16 to 17 degrees, young or with a few years, with grilled lamb, pork with prunes, moussaka or a hard sheep's cheese.
The same blend aged under the national Reserve term: leather, dried fig and tobacco join the fruit and the wine takes on some of Naoussa's gravity without losing its flesh.
Rare, made by a few estates under the regional PGI: dark, soft, warm and plummy, low in acid, a wine that shows at once why it is the blending grape and not the lead.
Roditis, Assyrtiko and Malagousia from the same estates, fresh and uncomplicated, the house whites of the district's tavernas.

made.viticulture: Two grapes with different habits share the slopes. Xinomavro ripens late and carries tannin and acid it must be coaxed to soften; Negoska is vigorous, generous and ripens more easily, so its yield must be held down or it dilutes the blend. Most vineyards are on wires in cordon or Guyot, with older bush-vine plots in the villages; rows run along the contours of the foothills, and the canopy is opened to the Vardaris so bunches dry after a shower. Harvest comes from mid-September for Negoska to early October for Xinomavro, by hand, and the two are often grown in the same vineyard and picked a fortnight apart. The hazards are the usual Macedonian ones, a wet spring, mildew, hail, and a cold snap off the north; the warmth of the lower ground means drought stress on the sandier soils in a hot August. A number of the district's small estates farm organically.
made.winemaking: The blend is the craft. Some houses ferment the two grapes together, letting Negoska's colour and softness go into Xinomavro from the first day; more pick them separately, ferment each in steel or open vats with a maceration of two to three weeks, and assemble after malolactic with Negoska at a fifth to a third. Maturation is in oak, French barriques and larger casks both, for a year or so in the ordinary wine and longer under the Reserve and Grande Reserve terms, which are the national ones. The aim is a wine that drinks within a few years, so new oak is used sparingly and extraction is gentler than in the traditional Naoussa school. A few growers work with wild yeasts and little sulphur and bottle without fining or filtration, which has given the small district a following out of proportion to its size.

law.classification: Goumenissa is a protected designation of origin established in 1979 for dry red wine from a delimited zone on the Paiko foothills in the Kilkis regional unit. It is the only Macedonian Xinomavro appellation that requires a blend: Xinomavro with Negoska, and the law sets a floor of 20% Negoska, so the senior grape may not exceed 80%. No white, rosé or sparkling wine may use the name, and the national Reserve and Grande Reserve ageing terms apply. The district's other wines, varietal Negoska, Roditis and Assyrtiko whites and international blends, are sold as PGI Macedonia.

Dry red from Xinomavro and Negoska grown on the Paiko foothills in Kilkis, with Negoska at least 20% of the blend.
Goumenissa Reserve
The national Reserve term for PDO reds, Epilegmenos: extended ageing in oak and bottle before release.
Goumenissa Grande Reserve
The national Grande Reserve term, Eidika Epilegmenos: four years' ageing at least, divided between oak and bottle.
PGI Macedonia
The regional wine for the district's varietal Negoska, its whites and any blend with international grapes.

places.name: Mount Paiko
places.note: The broad, wooded mountain north-west of Thessaloniki whose south-eastern foothills hold the whole appellation; its slopes fall to the Axios plain and take the morning sun.

places.name: Goumenissa
places.note: The market town at the centre of the zone, a place of mills and brass bands with vineyards on the slopes above it; most of the district's family estates and the largest house's winery are here or close by.

places.name: Griva
places.note: A village in the Paiko foothills a few kilometres from the town, with older plantings of both grapes on stonier, higher ground.

places.name: Filyria
places.note: A village of the zone whose name the district's largest house prints on its best-known Goumenissa, a blend of Xinomavro and Negoska aged in oak.

places.name: The Axios plain
places.note: The flat land east of the zone, the valley of the river the north calls the Vardar; its wind, the Vardaris, dries the vineyards, and its warmth marks the lower edge of the appellation.

producers.name: Boutari
producers.why: The Naoussa house has made Goumenissa for decades and introduced most of Greece to the Xinomavro and Negoska blend; its Filiria Goumenissa is the district's best-known label.

producers.name: Aidarinis
producers.why: A family estate in the town whose Goumenissa and old-vine bottlings are the traditional reference for the appellation's blend.

producers.name: Chatzivaritis
producers.why: An organic family estate at Goumenissa with a wide range from the appellation blend to varietal Negoska and Roditis, a good study of the district's grapes one by one.

producers.name: Tatsis
producers.why: A small Goumenissa estate working with wild yeasts, little sulphur and no filtration, whose Xinomavro and Negoska wines carried the appellation onto natural wine lists abroad.

exam: The blending rule: Xinomavro with at least 20% Negoska, the one Macedonian Xinomavro appellation that must blend.
Negoska: where its name comes from, what it adds, colour, alcohol and softness, and that it is grown almost nowhere else.
The place: Kilkis, Mount Paiko, north-west of Thessaloniki, above the Axios plain; lower and warmer than Naoussa.
The date, 1979, and the style: rounder and readier than Naoussa, darker in the glass.
The four Xinomavro appellations in one line: Naoussa alone, Amyndeon alone with rosé and sparkling, Goumenissa with Negoska, Rapsani with Krassato and Stavroto.
traps: The 20% is a floor on Negoska, not a cap: a Goumenissa may carry more Negoska, and Xinomavro may not exceed 80%.
Negoska takes its name from Naoussa's old Slavic name, Negush, yet it is not permitted in Naoussa; it belongs to Goumenissa.
Goumenissa is in Kilkis on Mount Paiko, not on Vermio with Naoussa and Amyndeon; the three districts are neighbours, not one zone.
Red only: there is no Goumenissa rosé or white, whatever the estate also makes under PGI Macedonia.
Negoska and Negroamaro of Puglia sound alike and are unrelated; do not let the sound carry you to Italy.

cards.f: Goumenissa: the grape rule
cards.b: Xinomavro blended with Negoska, Negoska at least 20%; dry red only. The one Macedonian Xinomavro appellation that must blend.

cards.f: Negoska: origin of the name and what it brings
cards.b: From Negush, the old Slavic name of Naoussa. Deep colour, lower acid, higher alcohol, soft tannin: the flesh Xinomavro lacks. Grown almost only at Goumenissa.

cards.f: Where is Goumenissa?
cards.b: Kilkis regional unit, Central Macedonia, north-west of Thessaloniki, on the south-eastern foothills of Mount Paiko above the Axios plain; lower and warmer than Naoussa.

cards.f: Goumenissa: appellation date and style in the glass
cards.b: 1979. Medium ruby, deeper than Naoussa: sour cherry, plum, tomato leaf, spice, fresh acid, rounder tannin; drinks within a few years.

cards.f: The four Xinomavro appellations and their partners
cards.b: Naoussa: alone. Amyndeon: alone, with rosé and sparkling. Goumenissa: Negoska at least 20%. Rapsani, Thessaly: Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts.

cards.f: The wind of Goumenissa and what it does
cards.b: The Vardaris, the cold north wind down the Axios valley: dries the vineyards after rain, checks rot, and can chill the spring.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least 20% of a wine labelled Goumenissa?
questions.exp: Goumenissa is Xinomavro blended with at least 20% Negoska. Krassato and Stavroto are Rapsani's partners for Xinomavro, and Limnio is an ancient red of Lemnos and Chalkidiki.

questions.q: On the foothills of which mountain do the vineyards of Goumenissa lie?
questions.exp: Goumenissa sits on Mount Paiko in Kilkis. Vermio holds Naoussa and Amyndeon, Olympus holds Rapsani, and Athos is the monastic peninsula of Chalkidiki.

questions.q: In which year was Goumenissa established as an appellation?
questions.exp: Goumenissa came in 1979, eight years after Naoussa and seven after Amyndeon, the last of the three Macedonian Xinomavro appellations.

questions.q: What does Negoska chiefly contribute to the Goumenissa blend?
questions.exp: Negoska is deep-coloured, lower in acid, higher in alcohol and soft in tannin, filling out what Xinomavro lacks; acidity and tannin are Xinomavro's own contribution.

questions.q: In which regional unit of Greece does Goumenissa lie?
questions.exp: Goumenissa is in Kilkis, north-west of Thessaloniki. Imathia holds Naoussa, Florina holds Amyndeon, and Pella lies between them around Edessa.

questions.q: From the old Slavic name of which Greek wine town does the grape Negoska take its name?
questions.exp: Negush was the old Slavic name of Naoussa, so Negoska means the grape of Naoussa; the irony is that Naoussa's appellation does not permit it and Goumenissa requires it.

questions.q: Which style of wine may carry the Goumenissa name?
questions.exp: Goumenissa, like Naoussa and Rapsani, is dry red only. Of the Xinomavro appellations only Amyndeon admits rosé and sparkling wine.

questions.q: What is the largest share of the blend Xinomavro may take in a Goumenissa?
questions.exp: Negoska must be at least 20%, so Xinomavro may reach 80% at most; a 100% Xinomavro from Macedonia is Naoussa or Amyndeon.

regions.name: Rapsani
regions.summary: Rapsani is the Xinomavro appellation of Thessaly and the odd one out: a blend of three grapes, Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto, in equal shares, grown on the south-eastern lower slopes of Mount Olympus above the Vale of Tempe and within sight of the Aegean. An appellation since the first decrees of 1971, it fell near to abandonment before a large Macedonian house revived it in the 1990s, and a few estates have since followed. Iron-rich schist, terraces climbing the mountain and the sea's breath give a red fuller and warmer than Naoussa, with red fruit, spice and earth over Xinomavro's acid and a tannin rounded by its two partners. The exam asks the three grapes and the mountain.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean with the mountain's correction: hot, dry summers on the lower terraces, cooler air and later ripening higher up, and the Aegean a few kilometres to the east sending breezes up the slope in the afternoon. Olympus shelters the vineyards from the north-west and gathers cloud on its summit while the terraces stay in sun. Rain falls mostly in winter; drought on the thin schist is the summer hazard and a wet harvest the autumn one.
terroir.soils: Weathered schist and slate, stony, thin and poor, stained red with iron, with pockets of sandstone and gravel: a soil that drains instantly, limits vigour and gives the wine its earthy, mineral stamp. Iron-rich weathered schist is the phrase to attach to Rapsani in an exam.
terroir.topography: Terraced vineyards on the eastern and south-eastern foot of Olympus, Greece's highest mountain at 2,917 metres, climbing from the village of Rapsani and the edge of the Vale of Tempe up the lower slopes; altitude and the mix of schist and aspect vary from terrace to terrace, so the three grapes were traditionally planted together and picked as the site allowed.
terroir.water: The Pinios river cuts the Vale of Tempe between Olympus and Mount Ossa just south of the vineyards on its way to the Aegean, and the sea itself lies close enough to be seen from the upper terraces; both temper the heat of the Thessalian summer.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.styles: A third of the blend by rule: the acid, the tannin and the dried-rose and tomato perfume, ripening a little riper on these warm schist terraces than in Macedonia.

grapes.name: Krassato
grapes.styles: A local red, a third of the blend, that brings alcohol, body and roundness to Xinomavro's frame; it is grown almost nowhere else.

grapes.name: Stavroto
grapes.styles: The third grape, also local, adding colour and a softer, fleshier tannin; like Krassato it is barely seen outside Rapsani.

wines.note: Medium ruby, deeper than Naoussa, with sour cherry, raspberry, dried tomato, thyme and sweet spice over an earthy, iron-tinged base; medium-plus acid, rounded tannin and a warmer, fuller frame. Serve at 16 to 17 degrees with roast lamb with herbs, grilled sausages, aubergine dishes or a hard cheese.
The blend aged under the national Reserve term: tobacco, leather and dried fig join the fruit, and the schist's earthiness comes forward. The style the reviving house made famous in the 1990s.
Four years at least between cask and bottle; dried flowers, tar and dried tomato on a mellow frame, Rapsani's answer to old Naoussa and a bottle for slow-roasted meat.
The regional wines of the estates: varietal Xinomavro, Limniona and international grapes from Thessaly's vineyards, sold outside the appellation.

made.viticulture: The old vineyards of Rapsani were field blends: the three grapes planted together as bush vines on dry-stone terraces, picked together and fermented together, which is where the equal-parts rule came from. Many of those terraces were abandoned in the middle of the twentieth century as the village emptied, and the revival of the 1990s replanted on wires in cordon and Guyot, often with each variety in its own block so it can be picked at its own moment. The schist is thin and poor, so vigour is low and yields are small without much effort; the summer hazard is drought, met with careful canopy management on the old terraces, and the sea breeze helps the bunches through August. Harvest runs through September into early October, by hand, with Xinomavro the last to come in.
made.winemaking: Each grape plays a part. Xinomavro gives acid and tannin, Krassato alcohol and body, Stavroto colour and softness, and the appellation asks for them in equal shares, so the winemaker either ferments a field blend together or vinifies three lots and assembles them. Maceration runs two to three weeks in steel or open vats, malolactic follows, and the wine goes to oak, French barriques for the estates and larger casks for the traditional style, for a year in the ordinary wine and for the national minimums in Reserve and Grande Reserve. The reviving house built the appellation's modern name on a Reserve and a Grande Reserve, and the newer estates make brighter, less oaked versions that show the schist. There is no white, rosé or sweet Rapsani; everything else goes out as PGI Thessaly.

law.classification: Rapsani is a protected designation of origin from the first Greek decrees of 1971, for dry red wine from a delimited zone of terraces around the village of Rapsani on the slopes of Olympus in the Larissa regional unit of Thessaly. The blend is fixed: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts, which makes it the only one of the four Xinomavro appellations with three grapes and the only one outside Macedonia. The national Reserve and Grande Reserve ageing terms apply. The appellation ranks no vineyard, and the estates' other wines are PGI Thessaly.
tiers: Rapsani PDO
Dry red from Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal shares, grown on the terraces of Olympus around Rapsani in Thessaly.
Rapsani Reserve
The national Reserve term for PDO reds, Epilegmenos: extended ageing in oak and bottle before release.
Rapsani Grande Reserve
The national Grande Reserve term, Eidika Epilegmenos: four years' ageing at least, divided between oak and bottle.
PGI Thessaly
The regional wine of the whole of Thessaly, for the estates' varietals and blends outside the appellation.

places.name: Mount Olympus
places.note: Greece's highest mountain, 2,917 metres at its summit, the home of the ancient gods; the appellation lies on its eastern and south-eastern foot, far below the snow, where the schist terraces catch the sun and the sea air.

places.name: Rapsani
places.note: The village that names the appellation, on the lower slopes above the Vale of Tempe, once a prosperous wine village that emptied in the twentieth century and was replanted from the 1990s.

places.name: The Vale of Tempe
places.note: The gorge of the Pinios between Olympus and Ossa, the ancient road from Macedonia into Thessaly, just south of the vineyards; the river and the sea beyond it cool the lower terraces.

places.name: Mount Ossa and Ambelakia
places.note: Across the Vale, Ossa faces Olympus, and the village of Ambelakia on its slope, little vineyards in Greek, grew rich on red dye rather than wine; a name to keep apart from Rapsani.

producers.name: Tsantali
producers.why: The large Macedonian house that revived Rapsani in the 1990s, replanting the terraces and making the Reserve and Grande Reserve the appellation's calling cards for a generation.

producers.name: Dougos
producers.why: A family estate at Rapsani whose Rapsani and whose varietal wines from the same slopes put a grower's name beside the large house on the Olympus terraces.

producers.name: Thymiopoulos Vineyards
producers.why: The Naoussa estate's Rapsani Terra Petra, from the three grapes on the schist, is the bottle most Advanced candidates taste for the appellation.

exam: The three grapes in equal shares: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto; the only three-grape Xinomavro appellation and the only one outside Macedonia.
The place: Thessaly, Larissa, the slopes of Olympus, the Vale of Tempe, the Aegean close by.
The soil phrase: iron-rich weathered schist.
The history: the 1971 decree, decline, revival from the 1990s by a large Macedonian house, the estates since.
The style against Naoussa: fuller, warmer, rounder, deeper in colour, with earth and herbs.
traps: Rapsani is in Thessaly, not Macedonia; it is the one Xinomavro appellation south of the Macedonian border, and Olympus is its mountain, not Vermio.
Three grapes, not one: a 100% Xinomavro from these slopes cannot be Rapsani.
Krassato and Stavroto are Rapsani's partners; Negoska is Goumenissa's. Do not swap them in a blend question.
Ambelakia, across the Vale of Tempe on Ossa, means little vineyards and is a dye town, not a wine appellation.
Olympus the mountain is in Thessaly and Macedonia; Olympia, the sanctuary of the games, is in the western Peloponnese, nowhere near Rapsani.

cards.f: Rapsani: the three grapes and their shares
cards.b: Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts, a third each. Dry red only.

cards.f: Rapsani: where it lies
cards.b: Thessaly, Larissa regional unit, on the eastern and south-eastern lower slopes of Mount Olympus above the Vale of Tempe, a few kilometres from the Aegean.

cards.f: What each grape brings to Rapsani
cards.b: Xinomavro: acid, tannin, dried rose and tomato. Krassato: alcohol, body, roundness. Stavroto: colour and a softer tannin.

cards.f: Rapsani's soil in two words, and its effect
cards.b: Iron-rich schist: thin, stony, quick-draining, low vigour; gives the wine its earthy, mineral stamp and its warmer, fuller frame beside Naoussa.

cards.f: Rapsani's history in one line
cards.b: Appellation in 1971; terraces abandoned as the village emptied; revived in the 1990s by a large Macedonian house; a few estates since, with Reserve and Grande Reserve as the calling cards.

cards.f: Rapsani against Naoussa in the glass
cards.b: Rapsani: deeper colour, fuller, warmer, rounder tannin, red fruit, thyme, earth. Naoussa: paler, higher acid, firmer tannin, tomato and olive, longer-lived.

questions.q: Which three grapes make up a wine labelled Rapsani?
questions.exp: Rapsani is Xinomavro with the two local grapes Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts. Negoska belongs to Goumenissa, Agiorgitiko to Nemea, and blends with Merlot or Syrah are regional PGI wines.

questions.q: On the slopes of which mountain is Rapsani grown?
questions.exp: Rapsani lies on the eastern foot of Mount Olympus in Thessaly. Vermio holds Naoussa and Amyndeon, Paiko holds Goumenissa, and Pelion is the peninsula south-east of Volos.

questions.q: In which region of Greece does the Rapsani appellation lie?
questions.exp: Rapsani is the Xinomavro appellation of Thessaly, in the Larissa regional unit; the other three Xinomavro appellations are all in Macedonia.

questions.q: What share of a Rapsani blend does the appellation set for each of its three grapes?
questions.exp: The decree fixes Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto in equal shares, a third each. A 20% floor is Goumenissa's rule for Negoska, and Naoussa is Xinomavro alone.

questions.q: Which soil is the signature of Rapsani's terraces?
questions.exp: Rapsani's terraces are weathered, iron-stained schist, thin and poor. Volcanic ash and pumice is Santorini, red clay is Nemea's valley floor, and deep alluvial silt is plain-country soil, not a terrace on Olympus.

questions.q: Which house replanted Rapsani's abandoned terraces on Olympus and revived the appellation?
questions.exp: Tsantali took up the abandoned Olympus terraces in the 1990s and made Rapsani Reserve and Grande Reserve the appellation's calling cards for a generation. Boutari is Naoussa's old house, Skouras is a Peloponnese estate near Argos, and Alpha Estate belongs to the Amyndeon plateau.

questions.q: In which decade was Rapsani revived after years of neglect?
questions.exp: A large Macedonian house replanted the Olympus terraces and relaunched Rapsani in the 1990s; the appellation itself dates from 1971, but the vineyards had largely been abandoned.
